enrichment.short_title: Arbitrators exceeded powers by ignoring contract currency and Lesotho interest law
key_facts: LHDA and the Highlands Water Venture consortium disputed extra-cost claims from construction of the Katse Dam in Lesotho under FIDIC-style conditions governed by Lesotho law, with ICC arbitration seated in London.

The arbitral tribunal awarded sums in European currencies rather than the contractually stipulated Maloti/rand and foreign currency proportions, and applied English procedural discretion on interest under section 49 rather than Lesotho ex mora substantive law.

Morison J remitted the currency and interest issues under section 68 as serious irregularity (excess of powers); HWV appealed, arguing sections 48(4) and 49(3) gave the tribunal freestanding discretion even where the contract and applicable law dictated otherwise.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a Commercial Court order remitting parts of an ICC partial award under section 68 of the Arbitration Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge was entitled to remit the currency and interest issues for reconsideration.
enrichment.ratio: Where a contract clearly fixes currency of account and payment proportions, section 48(4) restates rather than overrides the substantive obligation to award in the contract currencies; where the applicable law (Lesotho Roman-Dutch law) gives a substantive ex mora right to interest, section 49(3) does not authorise the tribunal to apply English procedural discretion instead, and departing from the contract on these matters is an excess of power under section 68(2)(b).
legal_issues: Whether currency of an arbitral award is governed by procedural or substantive law
Whether sections 48(4) and 49(3) override express contractual currency provisions
Whether awards of interest in civil-law-governed contracts are substantive or lex fori matters
Whether the tribunal exceeded its powers within section 68(2)(b)

enrichment.short_title: Suspended committal set aside for breach of committal Practice Direction safeguards

statutes_considered.title: Civil Procedure Rules 1998
provisions: Committal Applications Practice Direction Part I and Part II

key_facts: Amberley Construction obtained a £7,500 judgment against Paul Beamish, a project manager, who failed to pay and gave misleading information about his bank accounts at a judgment-debtor examination.

Judge Kennedy convened Beamish on two days' notice, examined him himself without prior written specification of the alleged contempts, and imposed a concurrent 28-day suspended committal at the same hearing.
Beamish was unrepresented; the claimant was not notified of the hearing; no opportunity was given to take legal advice or prepare a defence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a county court suspended committal order for contempt in the face of the court during judgment-debt enforcement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Judge Kennedy's committal order set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Committal for contempt in the face of the court must comply with the Committal Applications Practice Direction, including detailed written notice of alleged conduct, reasonable time to respond and obtain legal advice, and a separate opportunity to address penalty; serious procedural breaches that prejudice an unrepresented contemnor require the order to be set aside as incompatible with Article 6.
legal_issues: Whether committal procedures were used impermissibly to enforce a private judgment debt
Whether the contemnor was adequately informed of the acts of contempt
Whether Part II of the Committal Practice Direction was complied with
Whether Article 6 fair trial rights were breached by judicial interrogation without self-incrimination warning

enrichment.short_title: Business partner appeal allowed after late contract amendment without further cross-examination
key_facts: Mrs Amos and Mr Bowerbank jointly built a trade magazine business through Paparazzi and subsidiary companies with a concealed 70/30 beneficial share split.

When Amos became seriously ill in November 1998 she transferred legal title to shares and granted a power of attorney; Bowerbank then licensed Paparazzi's database and titles to his own company Castle while Integrated went into liquidation.

After a prolonged county court trial framed as breach of trust, the judge found for Amos on facts but against her on law, then permitted a very late amendment to add an oral agreement to sell or refinance the business, refused further cross-examination of Amos, and awarded about £18,639 plus interest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from Central London County Court after a part-heard trial with permission to appeal on amendment, refusal of adjournment, judgment, and costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; judgment and costs order set aside; case remitted to the trial judge for further cross-examination of Amos and reassessment of liability and quantum.
enrichment.ratio: Granting permission to amend at the end of trial from a trust claim to a contract claim did not offend the Barrell jurisdiction, but once the new case was pleaded justice required the defendant be allowed further to cross-examine on essential contract terms; damages for breach of the oral agreement must be measured by what Amos would have received if Bowerbank had performed, not by an arbitrary asset valuation at 5 January 1999.
legal_issues: Whether post-judgment amendment was permissible under Barrell Enterprises principles
Whether refusal to adjourn for further cross-examination was unjust
Whether trust-based pleading failure should defeat the claim after favourable fact findings
Correct measure of damages for breach of the alleged November 1998 oral agreement

enrichment.short_title: Luton post office murder convictions quashed after cumulative prosecution disclosure failures
key_facts: David Cooper and Michael McMahon were convicted in 1970 of murdering sub-postmaster Reginald Stevens in Luton; the prosecution case depended heavily on accomplice witness Alfred Mathews.

enrichment.procedural_posture: Reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission to the Court of Appeal under section 17 Criminal Appeal Act 1968; appeals against conviction long after original trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; convictions quashed as unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: Applying Pendleton, where cumulative fresh and undisclosed material—including misleading presentation of Good's role, Edwards' credible exculpatory evidence as to Murphy affecting assessment of Mathews, McNair's identification evidence, and undisclosed earlier statements of Mrs Mathews—undermines the critical witness, the court itself must regard the convictions as unsafe even if each point alone might not be decisive.
legal_issues: Safety of conviction standard after Pendleton
Impact of Murphy's successful appeal on co-accused
Material nondisclosure relating to Good and Mrs Mathews
Whether prior Court of Appeal reasoning on Mathews' credibility remained valid

enrichment.short_title: Accountants liable for failing to advise Channel Islands salary routing for non-domiciled banker
key_facts: Mr Slattery, an Irish/Canadian Citibank executive resident but not ordinarily resident in the UK, was paid net salary into a London account while working partly abroad.

Moore Stephens prepared tax returns apportioning foreign earnings and claiming large PAYE refunds on the assumption he was paid abroad, without advising him to use a Jersey account available to other Citibank employees.
When Slattery disclosed UK payment in 1999 he had to repay about £310,000 to HMRC; he sued for the tax savings he could have made with proper advice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Chancery trial of a professional negligence claim against chartered accountants for UK tax advice and return preparation.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Slattery for £197,092.48 damages; breach established for 1996/97 and 1997/98 with 50% contributory negligence reducing the latter year's recovery.
enrichment.ratio: A reasonably competent tax adviser owed a duty to tell a resident non-domiciled employee frequently working abroad that payment into a Channel Islands account would avoid deemed remittance of foreign earnings; Moore Stephens breached that duty and caused loss for 1996/97, and Slattery's failure to query an unexpected £127,000 refund amounted to 50% contributory negligence for 1997/98 but did not break causation entirely.
legal_issues: Scope of Moore Stephens' retainer and duty to advise on offshore payment
Whether October 1996 telephone advice to pay salary in New York was given
Causation and loss for each tax year
Contributory negligence and break in chain of causation on large unexpected refund

enrichment.short_title: Porcelain supplier's confidentiality, copyright and purchase-order IP rights upheld at preliminary issue
key_facts: A Middle Eastern tableware wholesaler and Derby porcelain manufacturer Lynton traded for years under exclusive distributorship agreements (1990 and 1996) under which the wholesaler presented itself as manufacturer and owned commissioned designs.
The 1996 agreement terminated by consent in June 2001; the wholesaler continued placing orders on standard purchase order terms assigning IP and restricting use of customer/end-user information.
The wholesaler sued alleging breach of confidence, copyright in back stamps and patterns, and retention of paid-for moulds; Lynton broadly denied subsistence of rights.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited trial of preliminary issues on nature and extent of contractual, equitable and copyright rights before the main breach/infringement trial.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issues largely resolved in favour of the claimant on subsistence of confidence and copyright and ownership of moulds; clause 11.1 contractual confidentiality did not survive termination but equitable duties continued.
enrichment.ratio: The fact that named or crest-identified customers/end-users of bespoke tableware are clients of the wholesaler is confidential information not defeated by springboard arguments; simplified crest artwork and composite back-stamp layouts involve sufficient skill and labour for copyright as graphic works; post-termination purchase orders incorporated terms assigning design copyright to the buyer and restricting disclosure of customer identity.
legal_issues: Whether preliminary issue trial could determine confidentiality without knowing what information was misused
Construction of clause 11.1 1996 agreement as surviving termination
Whether purchase order terms were incorporated after termination
Subsistence of copyright in back stamps and decorative patterns
Ownership of commissioned moulds

enrichment.short_title: Seller granted summary judgment where loadport inspector certificate was final and binding
key_facts: Exxonmobil sold 15,000 mt ultra low sulphur diesel cif Cardiff to Texaco under a contract making SGS loadport certificates final and binding save fraud or manifest error.
SGS certified compliance at Gravenchon including minimum 58°C flashpoint, but discharge-port testing led Texaco to reject the cargo as off-specification.
Exxonmobil treated rejection as repudiatory, resold the cargo, and sought damages exceeding US$785,000 plus demurrage.

enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment for Exxonmobil on liability; no permission to defend; declaration that clause 20 did not exclude section 50 damages; judgment for US$60,100 demurrage.
enrichment.ratio: Part I clause 6's independent-inspector regime prevailed over conflicting Part II clause 2.4 sampling provisions so Texaco could not rely on an express/implied obligation to retain sample portions from the superseded procedure; the entire agreement clause excluded implied terms based on usage or custom; loss of prospective profits wording in clause 20 did not bar section 50 market-price damages.

Whether failure to retain sample portions invalidated the SGS certificate

enrichment.short_title: Care threshold upheld where mother declined to give evidence; child witness refusal within discretion
key_facts: Care proceedings concerned Michael (born 1988) and Lola (born 1990) after alleged assaults by their mother, including a July 2002 electric flex injury to Lola's hand.
The mother had a 1998 conviction for assaulting both children with an electric flex; supervision orders had previously returned the children to her care.
The mother filed written denials but declined to give oral evidence; Michael, separately represented, was refused permission to give oral evidence supporting the mother's account.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court (Family Division) from a district judge's threshold findings under section 31 Children Act 1989 in care proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: In care proceedings a parent who declines to give evidence should usually be taken as unable to rebut allegations proved on other evidence; separately, refusal to permit a 14-year-old separately represented child to give oral evidence was within the district judge's welfare-based discretion where trauma and conflict with his sister's account outweighed potential benefit.
legal_issues: Inference from parent's failure to give oral evidence in care cases
Whether Michael should have been permitted to give evidence
Compatibility with Article 6 of refusing child witness while relying on hearsay
Whether section 31 threshold was met on alleged assaults

enrichment.short_title: No binding Formula One title sponsorship deal on alleged Vodafone phone call
key_facts: Jordan Grand Prix claimed that in a 10–15 minute telephone call on 22 March 2001 Eddie Jordan and Vodafone global brand director David Haines orally agreed a US$150m title sponsorship for seasons 2002–2004.

Complex written negotiations were ongoing; key terms including livery, bonuses, intellectual property and renewal options remained unresolved and both sides expected board approval and written contracts.
Vodafone ultimately sponsored Ferrari instead; Jordan also pursued an alternative misrepresentation claim relating to its negotiations with Gallaher.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Commercial Court trial of breach of contract and misrepresentation claims arising from alleged oral sponsorship agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed in full; no binding contract and alternative misrepresentation claim failed.
enrichment.ratio: A contract of this magnitude cannot be formed on a brief telephone conversation where essential commercial terms were unsettled and both parties understood any agreement required written board-approved documentation; Haines had neither actual nor ostensible authority to bind Vodafone Group, and the alleged representation was not acted upon nor shown to have caused loss.

Actual and ostensible authority of brand director to bind parent company
Application of First Energy principles to communication of board decisions

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review dismissed over preserved rights community care grant allocation

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: From April 2002 funding and care responsibility for residents with preserved rights to enhanced income support in independent care homes transferred from central government to local authorities.
The Secretary of State determined a fixed national pot (about £614m for England in 2002/03) and allocated grants by formula rather than reimbursing actual local authority expenditure.
Liverpool City Council received £8,640,683 but estimated a shortfall of about £1.45–2m against its additional costs and challenged inadequate consultation and irrationality.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of the Secretary of State for Health's section 93 Local Government Act 2000 determination of preserved-rights grants for 2002/03.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Determination upheld in relation to Liverpool's grant.
enrichment.ratio: Section 93(11) permits consultation with representative bodies such as the LGA and ADSS rather than every authority, and the consultation undertaken was genuine; determining fixed grants from estimated central savings to achieve broadly cost-neutral transfer was a rational policy choice and not rendered irrational by use of estimates or refusal to reimburse actual expenditure.
legal_issues: Adequacy of consultation under section 93(11) before determining grants
Whether failure to consult on size of national pot invalidated the Determination
Rationality of fixed-grant formula versus reimbursement mechanism
Whether Liverpool's shortfall demonstrated material miscalculation
